title: The Signature Lens: What 'Signature' Means for a Virus Record
t: The Signature Lens: What 'Signature' Means for a Virus Record
d: His rule: the public record stands untouched; the Signature line is his own framework laid beside it.
definition: His rule: the public record stands untouched; the Signature line is his own framework laid beside it.
description:
The Signature edition never rewrites the public record — the taxonomy, genome size and history stay exactly as documented. What it adds is his lens: how he organizes the knowledge, what patterns he sees across families, which questions he would ask next, and where his imagination goes when the facts run out. Every speculative sentence carries its label. The public record is the anchor; the Signature line is the sail. One holds, the other reaches.

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). Keep two columns: DOCUMENTED (facts with sources) and SIGNATURE (his frameworks, labeled speculative). Never let a sentence migrate columns without its label.

APPLICATIONS. A virus record that teaches both knowledge and intellectual honesty; the template for every Signature edition in the network.

title: Baltimore Classes as a Thinking Tool
t: Baltimore Classes as a Thinking Tool
d: His Signature take: the seven Baltimore classes are the periodic table of viruses.
definition: His Signature take: the seven Baltimore classes are the periodic table of viruses.
description:
David Baltimore's 1971 classification — seven classes by genome type and replication strategy — is, in his framing, the closest virology has to a periodic table. Class I (dsDNA) through VII (dsDNA-RT) predict how a virus must behave: a +ssRNA virus (Class IV) can be infectious as naked RNA; a -ssRNA virus (Class V) must carry its polymerase. His Signature lens: learn the class, and you can reason about any virus you've never met. The label stays: this is documented science, organized his way.

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). Teach each class as a 'replication contract': what the genome type forces the virus to bring, build, or steal.

APPLICATIONS. Faster reasoning about new viruses; the teaching ladder's backbone for the viruses database.

title: The Envelope Question
t: The Envelope Question
d: His framework: enveloped vs. non-enveloped predicts a virus's weaknesses.
definition: His framework: enveloped vs. non-enveloped predicts a virus's weaknesses.
description:
Enveloped viruses (influenza, coronaviruses, herpesviruses) wear a stolen lipid coat — which makes them vulnerable to soap, drying and disinfectants. Non-enveloped viruses (norovirus, poliovirus, adenovirus) are tougher environmental survivors. His Signature framing turns this into a rule of thumb: the coat is both armor and Achilles' heel. Documented virology; his organization. The practical upshot he stresses: this is why handwashing works on some viruses and barely dents others.

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). Sort every virus by envelope status first; derive its environmental toughness and disinfection logic from that single fact.

APPLICATIONS. Hygiene reasoning; disinfection strategy; a one-question triage for any virus.
how_it_works: Sort every virus by envelope status first; derive its environmental toughness and disinfection logic from that single fact.
applications: Hygiene reasoning; disinfection strategy; a one-question triage for any virus.

title: Genome Size and Lifestyle
t: Genome Size and Lifestyle
d: His observation: genome size predicts a virus's strategy.
definition: His observation: genome size predicts a virus's strategy.
description:
At ~1,700 bases, hepatitis D is a minimalist that must borrow everything. At ~300,000+ bases, giant viruses carry their own translation genes. His Signature lens: genome size is a lifestyle statement — small genomes mean dependence and efficiency; large genomes mean autonomy and complexity. Coronaviruses, with the largest RNA genomes (~30 kb), even carry a proofreading enzyme — the documented exception that proves the rule that RNA viruses mutate fast.

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). Plot families by genome size; read lifestyle (dependence vs. autonomy, mutation rate, host range) off the axis.

APPLICATIONS. A predictive habit for meeting new viruses; the 'size tells a story' lens.

title: Latency: The Viruses That Never Leave
t: Latency: The Viruses That Never Leave
d: His framework: herpesviruses as the model of negotiated coexistence.
definition: His framework: herpesviruses as the model of negotiated coexistence.
description:
Herpesviruses infect, then hide — latent in neurons or blood cells for life, reactivating under stress. His Signature reading: this is not a failed infection but a successful strategy, millions of years old. The virus trades virulence for permanence. He uses it as his model for thinking about persistence generally: in biology, in ideas, in systems. Documented science; his philosophical extension, labeled.

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). Study latency as strategy: what the virus gains by restraint, and what the host gains by tolerance.

APPLICATIONS. A model for persistence thinking; the philosophical core of his virus framework.

title: Ladder 1: What Is a Virus? (Simplest)
t: Ladder 1: What Is a Virus? (Simplest)
d: The simplest true explanation, built for a first meeting.
definition: The simplest true explanation, built for a first meeting.
description:
A virus is a package of instructions (DNA or RNA) wrapped in protein, sometimes with a fatty coat. It cannot eat, move, or reproduce on its own — it must enter a cell and use the cell's machinery to copy itself. Smaller than bacteria, invisible to ordinary microscopes, found everywhere life exists. His ladder rule: if a bright ten-year-old can't follow it, it's not ladder 1.

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). Start with the package metaphor; add one fact at a time; check understanding before climbing.

APPLICATIONS. The entry point of the teaching ladder; the explanation everything else builds on.
how_it_works: Start with the package metaphor; add one fact at a time; check understanding before climbing.

title: Ladder 2: How Viruses Copy Themselves (Compounded)
t: Ladder 2: How Viruses Copy Themselves (Compounded)
d: The middle rung: entry, replication, assembly, exit.
definition: The middle rung: entry, replication, assembly, exit.
description:
A virus lands on a cell, attaches to a receptor, and gets inside. Then it unpacks its genome and hijacks the cell: DNA viruses often head for the nucleus, RNA viruses may replicate in the cytoplasm, retroviruses write themselves into the host's DNA. New parts are built, assembled into fresh virions, and released — by bursting the cell or budding off politely. His ladder-2 rule: every virus does these four steps; the differences are in the details.

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). Teach the four-step cycle once, then show how each family customizes it.

APPLICATIONS. The compounded rung; the scaffold for understanding any specific virus.
how_it_works: Teach the four-step cycle once, then show how each family customizes it.
applications: The compounded rung; the scaffold for understanding any specific virus.

title: Ladder 3: Reading a Virus Like a Document (Most Complex)
t: Ladder 3: Reading a Virus Like a Document (Most Complex)
d: The top rung: genome, structure, and evolution as one readable system.
definition: The top rung: genome, structure, and evolution as one readable system.
description:
At ladder 3, a virus is a document written in nucleic acid, formatted by its capsid, and edited by evolution. You read its genome for the replication contract (Baltimore class), its structure for the delivery mechanism (envelope, spikes, symmetry), and its phylogeny for its history (spillovers, reassortments, adaptations). His most-complex rule: hold all three readings at once — the virus is only fully legible in stereo.

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). Combine genomics, structural biology and phylogenetics on a single record; practice on one virus until the three readings fuse.

APPLICATIONS. The expert rung; the full Signature reading of a virus record.

title: The Bacteriophage Corner: Viruses That Hunt Bacteria
t: The Bacteriophage Corner: Viruses That Hunt Bacteria
d: His Signature note: the most numerous entities on Earth deserve their own lens.
definition: His Signature note: the most numerous entities on Earth deserve their own lens.
description:
Bacteriophages — viruses that infect bacteria — may number 10^31 on the planet, more than every other organism combined. His Signature framing: phages are the ocean's immune system, the gut's gardeners, and molecular biology's founding tools. Documented science; his emphasis. He keeps a dedicated corner because a viruses database that only covers human pathogens is, in his words, 'a phone book with only one area code.'

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). Give phages equal standing: discovery (Twort/d'Hérelle), the plaque method, and their ecological role.

APPLICATIONS. Completeness of the virus concept; the non-human majority given its due.

title: Plant Viruses: The Original Discovery, Still Teaching
t: Plant Viruses: The Original Discovery, Still Teaching
d: His note: virology began with a sick tobacco plant — the database honors that.
definition: His note: virology began with a sick tobacco plant — the database honors that.
description:
Tobacco mosaic virus was the first virus discovered and the first crystallized, yet plant viruses remain the quiet majority of virology's history. His Signature lens: plants can't run from infection or call a doctor — their viruses reveal pure virus-plant coevolution, RNA silencing defenses, and agricultural stakes. Documented science; his framing keeps the founding story central.

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). Cover transmission (mechanical, vector), plant defenses (RNA silencing), and agricultural impact.

APPLICATIONS. The full kingdom coverage; the founding story kept alive.

t: Mirror Sweep: For Every Virus, Its Public Record

definition: His standing method applied: public facts first, Signature mirror second.

title: The Eradication Lesson: His Signature Reading
t: The Eradication Lesson: His Signature Reading
d: Smallpox as proof of what coordination can do.
definition: Smallpox as proof of what coordination can do.
description:
The documented facts: smallpox killed hundreds of millions; a global campaign erased it by 1980. His Signature reading: eradication is the strongest documented evidence that humanity can solve a planetary problem on purpose — with surveillance, a good tool (vaccine), and relentless coordination. He treats it as the existence proof behind his whole database program: if smallpox, why not ignorance?

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). Extract the method (surveillance + tool + coordination) and apply it as a template to other problems.

APPLICATIONS. The philosophical engine of the project; hope with a citation.

title: His Concept: The Virus as Information
t: His Concept: The Virus as Information
d: Speculative lens, labeled: viruses as messages, cells as readers.
definition: Speculative lens, labeled: viruses as messages, cells as readers.
description:
His Signature concept (speculative): strip away the biology and a virus is information that copies itself using other systems' machinery — closer to a rumor, a meme, or a computer virus than to a bacterium. Cells 'read' viral genomes the way computers run code. The concept's honesty: it's an analogy, not a mechanism — but analogies are how he thinks, and this one predicts real things (like why +ssRNA is infectious: it's already 'readable').

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). Use the information lens to predict: which genomes are directly infectious, why mutation rates differ, where antivirals should strike.

APPLICATIONS. A thinking tool for virology; the analogy that keeps paying rent.

title: His Concept: Spillover as Systems Failure
t: His Concept: Spillover as Systems Failure
d: Speculative lens, labeled: pandemics as the output of stressed interfaces.
definition: Speculative lens, labeled: pandemics as the output of stressed interfaces.
description:
His Signature concept (speculative): spillovers happen where stressed systems meet — deforestation pushing bats into farms (Nipah), live markets mixing species (SARS), dense cities meeting new pathogens. The virus is the spark; the tinder is the interface. The concept's honesty: ecology this complex resists single causes, and his lens is a way of looking, not a proven model. But it organizes the documented spillover stories into one pattern.

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). Map each emergence to its interface stress; look for the tinder, not just the spark.

APPLICATIONS. A pattern-language for emergence; prevention thinking aimed at interfaces.

title: His Concept: The Immune System as Archive
t: His Concept: The Immune System as Archive
d: Speculative lens, labeled: immunity as a living database.
definition: Speculative lens, labeled: immunity as a living database.
description:
His Signature concept (speculative): the adaptive immune system is a database — it archives encounters (memory cells), indexes threats (antibodies), and queries the archive on re-exposure (faster response). Vaccination is writing to the archive without paying the disease's price. The concept's honesty: immunologists use similar metaphors; his version is deliberate and labeled, and it connects his database program to biology's own.

title: Lineage Note: The ICTV Taxonomy
t: Lineage Note: The ICTV Taxonomy
d: His note on how virus names are actually governed.
definition: His note on how virus names are actually governed.
description:
Virus taxonomy is governed by the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV), which in recent years moved to a Linnaean-style system: realms, kingdoms, phyla, down to species — with binomial species names. Documented fact; his note explains why the database uses both classic family names (Coronaviridae) and the newer formal species names. His rule: use the names the field uses, note when they change.

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). Track ICTV updates per record; keep both common and formal names visible.

APPLICATIONS. Taxonomic hygiene; the database stays current as names evolve.

title: Lineage Note: Why Some Records Carry Two Names
t: Lineage Note: Why Some Records Carry Two Names
d: His convention for the old and new virus names.
definition: His convention for the old and new virus names.
description:

title: The Giant Virus Postscript
t: The Giant Virus Postscript
d: His note: the viruses that broke the definition.
definition: His note: the viruses that broke the definition.
description:
Mimivirus (2003) and its giant cousins carry 1,000+ genes, visible under light microscopes, with translation genes once thought exclusive to cells. Documented science; his postscript: every definition of 'virus' written before 2003 needs an asterisk. He keeps this note to remind the database that categories are provisional — the next discovery gets to edit the schema.

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). Reserve a 'definition-breakers' shelf; let anomalies edit the taxonomy, not just sit in it.

title: His Concept: Mutation as Drafting
t: His Concept: Mutation as Drafting
d: Speculative lens, labeled: viral evolution as rapid prototyping.
definition: Speculative lens, labeled: viral evolution as rapid prototyping.
description:
His Signature concept (speculative): an RNA virus mutating in a host population is running a draft-and-revise loop — thousands of variants, selection keeping what works. It's his 'boundless generator' made biological: generate variants, validate against reality (the immune system), keep the winners. The concept's honesty: evolution has no goals and his generator metaphor is his, but the generate-validate-keep loop is genuinely how both work.

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). Compare a virus's mutation strategy to a generator's settings: high mutation (fast drafts, many rejects) vs. proofreading coronaviruses (slow drafts, fewer rejects).

APPLICATIONS. A design lens on evolution; his generator philosophy reflected in biology.

title: The Soap Lesson: His Favorite Single Fact
t: The Soap Lesson: His Favorite Single Fact
d: One documented fact he would teach the whole world.
definition: One documented fact he would teach the whole world.
description:
Enveloped viruses — influenza, coronaviruses, RSV, measles — are destroyed by soap, because soap dissolves their lipid envelopes. Twenty seconds of handwashing dismantles them chemically. His Signature take: this is the highest leverage-to-effort ratio in all of public health, a documented fact that fits in one sentence. He keeps it as his favorite because it's proof that understanding a virus's structure is practical power.
